purpose: Inotersen is used to treat nerve damage caused by a rare inherited condition called hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR). This condition causes an abnormal protein called transthyretin to build up and damage nerves throughout your body. This medicine helps slow down or stop that nerve damage from getting worse.
how_it_works: Your liver makes a protein called transthyretin, and in people with this condition, a faulty gene causes the liver to make an abnormal version of that protein. Inotersen works like a tiny molecular 'off switch' — it targets the genetic message in your liver cells that tells them to make this harmful protein and blocks it. By reducing the amount of this bad protein your body produces, it helps protect your nerves from further damage.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include injection site reactions like redness, swelling, or bruising where you give yourself the shot. You may also experience nausea, headache, fatigue (feeling very tired), fever, chills, and flu-like symptoms. Some people notice swelling in their arms or legs.
warnings: This medicine carries two very important warnings. First, it can cause dangerously low platelet counts (called thrombocytopenia), which means your blood may not clot properly and you could have serious or life-threatening bleeding. Second, it can cause severe kidney problems. Because of these risks, you must have regular blood and urine tests while taking this medication, and it is only available through a special restricted program. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual bruising, bleeding, or changes in how much you urinate.
typical_dosing: Inotersen is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the stomach area, thigh, or upper arm. The typical dose is 284 mg injected once a week. Your healthcare team will teach you how to give yourself this injection at home. Try to take it on the same day each week to keep it consistent.
